title: Evaluate, adjust and implement factors influencing agricultural enterprises

lessons.title: Evaluating enterprise performance and its drivers
lessons.html:
From interpreting to evaluating

At NQF level 4 you move beyond recognising factors to evaluating how strongly each one affects an enterprise's results, deciding which can be adjusted, and implementing the changes.

Measure performance first

Use records to calculate key indicators per enterprise and compare them with targets, previous seasons and benchmarks from study groups or industry bodies:

  • Crops: yield per hectare, gross margin per hectare, cost per tonne, water use per tonne, percentage of class 1 product.
  • Livestock: calving or lambing percentage, weaning mass, mortality, feed conversion ratio, milk per cow, gross margin per large stock unit.
  • General: labour cost per unit, diesel per hectare, downtime.

Analyse the factors

CategoryQuestions to ask
NaturalWas rainfall, frost, heat or pest pressure unusual? How much yield was lost?
TechnicalWere cultivar choice, plant population, fertility, irrigation, breeding or nutrition right?
EconomicHow did input and product prices change? Interest costs?
MarketWere quality specs met? Were there rejections or price discounts?
HumanWere there skills gaps, labour shortages, absenteeism or late operations?
Legal and institutionalDid regulations, permits, export access or disease control measures affect the enterprise?

Controllable versus uncontrollable

Separate factors management can change (planting date, cultivar, stocking rate, timing of operations, marketing channel, training) from those it can only respond to (weather, world prices, exchange rate, disease outbreaks in the region). For uncontrollable factors, the response is risk management: insurance, diversification, reserves, contracts and flexible plans.

Prioritise

Rank factors by impact on profit and ease of change. Focus first on high-impact, controllable factors. A partial budget helps: list added income and reduced costs against reduced income and added costs for a proposed change.

lessons.title: Adjusting and implementing changes
lessons.html:
Designing adjustments

Examples of evidence-based adjustments:

  • Yields limited by soil acidity: implement a liming programme based on soil analysis.
  • High mortalities in weaners: review vaccination programme with the vet, improve shelter and nutrition.
  • Rejects due to bruising: retrain pickers, change crates, adjust bag fill levels.
  • Diesel per hectare rising: service tractors, match tractor size to implement, reduce passes.
  • Recurring drought losses: shift to drought-tolerant cultivars, reduce stocking rate, build fodder reserves.
  • Poor prices at the fresh produce market: develop a contract with a retailer or processor.

Partial budget example

Positive effectsRandNegative effectsRand
Extra income from higher yieldR90 000Cost of lime and spreadingR45 000
Reduced replant costsR10 000Extra labourR5 000
TotalR100 000TotalR50 000

Net benefit R50 000: the change is worthwhile if the assumptions are sound.

Implementing

  1. Get management approval and budget.
  2. Write a clear action plan: what, who, when, resources and expected results.
  3. Communicate the reason for the change to the team; people implement changes better when they understand why.
  4. Train workers where new skills are needed.
  5. Trial on a portion first where risk is high, with a comparison block.
  6. Roll out fully once results are confirmed.

Monitoring and review

Track the same indicators used in the evaluation so you can see whether the change worked. Record weather and other conditions so you can separate the effect of the change from external factors. Report results and adjust again if needed: evaluation and adjustment is a continuous cycle.

Compliance

Adjustments must stay within the law and standards: registered products used per label (Act 36 of 1947), animal disease control measures (Act 35 of 1984), labour and safety requirements and water use authorisations.

Key points

  • Measure enterprise performance against targets and benchmarks.
  • Analyse natural, technical, economic, market, human and legal factors.
  • Focus on high-impact controllable factors; manage risk for uncontrollable ones.
  • Use partial budgets to test proposed changes.
  • Implement with a plan, trial where risky, then monitor and review.
